newsitem.title: UK: UK rekindles hopes for new European military plane.
newsitem.headline: UK rekindles hopes for new European military plane.

text.p: Britain announced on Thursday it was rejoining a pan-European project to build a new military transport plane, the Future Large Aircraft (FLA).

Defence Secretary George Robertson said in a parliamentary statement Britain had decided to join at least five other European governments in inviting the Airbus Industrie consortium's new military arm to bid to develop and build the new aircraft.
The FLA project could be worth over $22 billion to the Airbus Military industry partners if their bid is successful and the governments decide to go ahead and order the aircraft.
"I have now decided that the UK should rejoin our European partners in issuing a Request for Proposals to Airbus Military Company for the Future Large Aircraft," Robertson said in his statement.

He emphasised that Britain would only go ahead with the project if the Airbus bid gave "value for money" and he was inviting the other participating governments to seek rival bids from other aircraft manufacturers.
But he said he was confident that Airbus would come up with acceptable proposals. "It looks as though the FLA is going to fly," he told a news conference.

"I am confident that Airbus, which competes everyday of the week with Boeing and with the other large aerospace suppliers (in the commercial aircraft market) and competes very successfully can confidently compete in this area as well," he told reporters.

Robertson said Britain was looking at a target price of around $75 million an aircraft, with Britain seeking up to 40 or 50 aircraft "over a fairly lengthy period of time", which would be part of a pan-European order for nearer 300 aircraft.
The FLA project was designed by the European aircraft industry to challenge U.S. firm Lockheed Martin's dominance of the market for tactical transport aircraft.
It was stuck on the drawing board for years due to lack of funding from sponsor governments but they got together at the Paris Airshow last month to revive the project as a commercial venture.

Because of the lack of development funds from member governments the pan-European consortium offered to treat the project like a commercial aircraft project, to be managed by Airbus with funding based on launch orders.

France, Germany, Italy, Spain and Turkey all gave their immediate go-ahead at the Paris meeting to making an official Request for Proposal (RFP), while Airbus said Britain was expected to join once the new Labour government had had time to consider the project.

Belgium and Portugal are also considering joining and Airbus executives said they were preparing the bid on the basis of the eight countries ordering around 291 aircraft, or six countries ordering 270.

A British government official confirmed on Thursday that other aircraft being considered by Britain included the C130J, the new version of the Lockheed Martin's Hercules, and the giant C17 strategic airlifter made by Boeing's new subsidiary McDonnell Douglas.

Britain's previous Conservative government awarded Lockheed a billion pound order in 1994 for 25 new C130Js but said it would consider buying the FLA to replace the balance of its fleet of old Hercules if the project was put on a commercial footing, the price was right and it was available in time.
FLA industrial partner British Aerospace Plc immediately welcomed Britain's move on Thursday.
"We welcome the open competition because we are confident that FLA will provide a first-class technical and value-for-money solution," said chief executive Sir Richard Evans.
"It is also a major step forward in European collaboration, offering a new approach to the procurement of complex military systems," he added.

Other members of the FLA industrial consortium include Airbus partners Aerospatiale of France, Daimler-Benz AG unit Daimler-Benz Aerospace (Dasa), and Spain's Construcciones Aeronauticas SA (CASA), as well as Finmeccanica of Italy's Alenia unit.
